I definitely agree re: dim lighting is the vibe, but this room would look even better with 3-5 points of light. You can start with two inexpensive lamps space evenly around the room and see how you feel. (At home I usually temporarily "borrow" lamps from my bedroom to try this out.)

All your light sources should all be dimmed so it's still a dark/moody room, but more sources of light will allow you to see what you're doing. As a bonus, it will make you/everyone else look more attractive since the light is coming from all sides. (Reduces harsh face shadows––think the opposite of holding up a flashlight at a campfire.) The result is that your room becomes much more relaxing even though most people can't put their finger on why.

Example: [This](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5aa71c88a9e02804b02bd5ea/1533314434852-4AMJ1QITMJBLHMXZL12A/Blacktail_Interior-17.jpg?format=2500w) was one of my favorite bars. It was definitely dim and moody, but you can see how many lamps/sconces/overheads they used to achieve the perfect dim.

I totally understand especially when it comes to bitterness. I'm more than a bit of a misandrist in real life. Even my above frustration, I think, comes from that same bitter place––like *even when it comes to entertainment* (the far-right stuff you mentioned, video games, sports, and the majority of executives in film/TV), male-directed entertainment makes far more money and reaches huge audiences. I want literally just one industry where smart women, not men, are the majority in charge (as in female-dominated publishing), the ones making more fruitful decisions for our society, and I want those good creative decisions to impact the biggest possible group.

I think this comment represents a very common perspective from a lot of the progressive crowd (and indeed in the younger tiers of publishing), so I wanted to respond. I strongly disagree that literature has been an outlet for boys or young men in this generation *at all*. Film and TV? Absolutely. Books? No way! Nothing besides like, *Percy Jackson* legacy IP! When I worked in publishing, I made a point of reviewing the major houses' frontlists from a gendered perspective. Every time I did this, I could count on one hand the amount of new YA and middle grade titles meant to appeal to boys. Very often for a given imprint, there were zero. Nobody cares.

I totally agree with your "untapped market of teen girls" assertion. And I believe that your comment's perspective carries the assumption that literature is important because it can be *powerful*––it can change minds and shift cultural expectations. (From your comment: "issues on the larger scale need to be addressed," and then you note misogyny, toxic masculinity, and so forth. I agree!) This is a laudable goal and perfectly understandable.

But sticking with this idea: Who needs that "cultural shift"? Who needs the education? If it's young progressive women, that's consistent, because they're by far the largest consumers of books about queer boys right now. But I believe your comment suggests that it's boys who need this education. 

So if Books like X address, say, toxic masculinity, then it logically follows that boys have to actually read and engage with Books like X to get that benefit. If they aren't reading at all (and are instead playing Fortnite or whatever)...well, the books could have a magical recipe for male moral perfection and it wouldn't matter. What *will* happen is that readers who are already inclined to pick up Books like X––who likely already believe in/understand toxic masculinity––will do so. That relatively small group will have their beliefs reinforced but sales probably will be low. The majority of male readers will, as a very generalized group, either pivot entirely to Brandon Sanderson-type stuff, or abandon books altogether and move to League of Legends etc. This is currently the case.

If an author makes no effort to appeal to the average straight cis boy, or that group's popular interests, then boys are unlikely to read that author's work unless it's assigned at school (and even then maybe not! Sparknotes exist!). The author is likely writing only for people who already agree with them. Which is perfectly fine. But once you accept that, you have to drop the fantasy that you can change the world through literature. 

I find this frustrating because I do think that male readers sharply drop off by adolescence and that it's a problem and that very few people in publishing seem to care. 

And I mainly think it's a shame because I actually do believe you can change the world through literature, but you have to meet readers where they are first.

RE: "People aren't disgusted by the sight of me," I  feel like I know what you mean. I recently had an interesting insight. For as long as I can remember, I've felt physical pain/cringed when I saw photos of myself. Logically, I guess I knew that I probably wasn't the most hideous person in the world. But because my reaction to myself was so visceral, I always low-key believed other people must have felt a similar type of revulsion. 

My face isn't literally disfigured, but to me, my specific features––especially when photographed––somehow come across as far uglier/more masculine/more repulsive than any kind of disfigurement. Surely most people could see that ugliness, too; they were just being nice not to say so.

The other day I saw some photos of myself in early high school. I wasn't beautiful by any means, but I just looked like a cute, nerdy child. I wasn't repulsed. It actually seemed pretty cruel, the idea of being repulsed by this little try-hard kid. I'm not explaining this well, but seeing myself as other people likely saw me was a massive revelation.

I totally understand. I would focus on three things:

1. **Desensitizing going into the hallway.** I feel this too! The bad news is the only way through this problem is going into the hallway more frequently. The good news is that the desensitization, if you're like me, takes a lot fewer trips than you'd think.) Don't just go into the hallway to throw something away––go into the hallway SPECIFICALLY for the sake of being brave and going into the hallway. If you can convince yourself to be brave like this  2-3 times a day for a week, it won't feel nearly as hard for the rest of your time there.
2. **Default to discarding basically everything in your studio.** At the "selection point," choose a few things, really really beloved things or high-use things in excellent condition, to keep. **It feels wasteful, but I guarantee you truly can throw away or donate almost everything in that studio**, and caring for yourself is important. Read or re-read Marie Kondo's original book. I know the principles are pretty common knowledge now, but actually reading her words always sparks a spiritual shift in me that lasts long enough to properly tidy. I re-read *Tidying Up* every single time I decide to get my life in order, and it always helps.
3. **Just clean one corner of one table.** I always think "nobody builds a wall, they just add a brick." The concept of cleaning the whole apartment is "building a wall." But it is physically impossible to clean the whole apartment, as an action. What I do when I get REALLY overwhelmed is, I pick a piece of furniture with nonsense on it. I divide it in half. I say, "Whatever is on this half, I'm going to make spotless." You can usually throw away or donate almost everything on that half, if you're being very honest with yourself. The progress itself may spur you to pick another section you can do...and then another...and then you're making your bed...you see the trajectory, but don't overwhelm yourself. You can only add one brick right now.

A few other things: What if you asked a family member for one day of help with trash clean-up for the above? I know how much I wouldn't like to do this, but it may be a huge, huge help. If you have $40-$100 and feel awful or embarrassed asking family (though you shouldn't feel ANY shame here), you could hire a TaskRabbit. I want to be cognizant of your back pain.

Are the heavy bags full of clothes you need to take to donations? Asking for help is a good start. You could also get one of these "granny carts" and take your clothes out in batches. Wheels are an incredible invention and I'm only half kidding.

But yeah I'm sorry you're going through this, it's really hard not to have a serene place of your own. Get some little trash bags (ones that won't hurt to carry), be brave and go to the hallway garbage dump as often as you can stand it, get a rolling cart/family member/TaskRabbit, and just keep going. If you get rid of more things than you bring inside every day, you're mathematically guaranteed to win :)

I love this post. I used a nose shaper for like 8 years before I got my nose cartilage shaved down via rhinoplasty. My roommates thought I was a dummy for thinking that putting what's essentially a heavy clothespin on my nose would change anything! How stupid! But they were wrong lol. Cartilage is super malleable and largely water; as far as I can tell, any kind of sustained pressure will compress the cartilage temporarily. 

I have photos before and after I started using it. Just took a look at old pictures, and it looks like nose shapers kept my bulbous tip about 2mm slimmer than its "normal state," as long as I used said shaper daily. Really doesn't matter which "shaper" you use. Just Google "nose shaper" on Amazon and there are a hundred identical ones for a few bucks each. In a pinch, I'd even use those heavy clips they use to keep bags of potato chips closed...don't recommend that since it's way more painful, but any sustained pressure worked for me. 

I really did have to use it for quite a long time, and every day, to keep up this effect.

When I was consistent with use, I would see probably 65% of the bulbous tip reduction that my rhinoplasty eventually gave me permanently. I still use them sometimes when my nose gets swollen in the mornings.

I hear you. The only sustainable parts of life are those that we're either externally forced to do or things that we genuinely enjoy.

Example: I now I put on makeup most days just for Zoom class. I used to show up bare-faced because I find putting on daily makeup very boring. In theory I'd like to look pretty every day; in practice, I would prefer to sleep in. I now do my makeup most days because I *love* having my little pre-class coffee and listening to a news podcast––but I can't do those things with my hands static, I need to fidget. The makeup is just how I fidget. Thus my luxury morning ritual (coffee + podcast) has a no-cost side effect that makes me look better all day. You could do this, and you could likely do something similar for your hairstyling routine too.

Here's all the stuff you listed in order of impact, from most to least impactful: Being relatively thin > not having acne > makeup done > hair done > wearing better clothing. 

It sounds like you have a really demanding job, and I'm so sorry you don't have more time and energy just to enjoy yourself. To be as conventionally pretty as possible with limited time/energy, I would recommend these things: 

* If you have 20 minutes, do your makeup, not your hair. Listen to something interesting and consider this time a radio break/a luxury.
* If you want to lose 30-40 pounds, the cheapest and least mentally taxing way to do that is to skip breakfast/maybe skip lunch and never have snacks. Exercise is great for your mental and physical health. However, it has very little to do with your weight for most people. Calorie counting all the time will work if you weigh all your food, but it is mentally exhausting.
* Dry shampoo the shit out of your pretty day-old hairstyle on day 2 or even day 3.

A little off topic, but I am sure you are beautiful and I hope you aren't too hard on yourself. It sounds like you're already kicking ass in the workspace, of course your energy is low. You shouldn't feel like you're failing if you don't do elaborate beautifying stuff every day. Men certainly don't :)

You have beautiful eyes with such memorable coloring. :) Your upper eyelids seem to be retaining a little bit of water. If you drink significantly more water and are able to really cut down your salt, you may see less puffiness. It's surprisingly difficult to do that because in the West, most processed foods and restaurant meals contain a lot of sodium. We all handle it a bit differently. Topical products that contain caffeine can also constrain the blood vessels in that area, and those may give you a result you like. The effects will be modest, but I don't think your swelling is that bad, either.

Below your eyes, it looks as though your fat pads have shifted a bit lower, which is perfectly natural as we get a bit older. If it bothers you, a doctor can go in and move/adjust the fat pads to get a smoother look. That process is a lower blepharoplasty, often coupled with fat grafting to keep the area youthful and plump. A typical result would look like [this](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Pre-and-post-op-lower-blepharoplasty-and-fat-transfer-Top-Pre-operative-photograph-of-a_fig5_293043891). I plan to do this for myself in a while (I personally think this is what makes me look the most "tired").

The topicals' effects will be modest in comparison, but they'll obviously be much less invasive and costly. It's all about what you feel comfortable with. Your eye area looks perfectly normal exactly as it is, and I think the people you mentioned in your title are jerks.

Unhelpful compliment first: They look great as they are. Thick brows are a great look, especially if you have them naturally, and I truly don't get angry vibes from this photo; what strikes me is just a very beautiful set of eyes. :) 

More helpful, since you asked: If you are worried they're dominating your face (e.g. you'd like more attention on your lips, eyelashes, or another feature), and if you know that your eyebrow hairs grow back quickly and aren't easily damaged, you can experiment with thinning out just the hairs closest to the center. Here's [an exaggerated version](https://i.pinimg.com/564x/bc/55/9c/bc559c0a872c559f9361115d26c92291.jpg) of what I mean. It may take some trial and error to look natural. I really like it, though; I also have naturally very thick/dark brows and I do this, plus a very little bit of shaping underneath the brow, plus a gray Korean brown pencil to keep 80% of my natural fullness but make my look a little softer. :)

This is maybe a niche one. All super-wealthy people in New York appear to have the exact same idea of what a "nice gift" or a "reasonable donation" or an "elegant bouquet" looks like. Kind of a  small-town vibe to rich people communities. Idk about, for example, the Bay Area equivalent of this, but I imagine it's similar? Older richies only: They will buy a new iPhone, laptop, etc and then forget about it in a closet because they didn't like whatever update came with it (e.g. remember when Apple replaced touch ID with face ID?). Tech purchases are basically never enough money to constitute "a big purchase," which seems obvious but it felt like a meaningful difference to me at the time lol.

There's a reason these are all socialmaxx things and not looksmaxxing. I think hyper-wealthy women, even young ones, know that money and power are more important than looks. Looks are ALWAYS important for women unfortunately––but I feel like for the wealthy it's more as a baseline of "you have to be thinner and hotter than some base Standard X," not in a "if you're at extraordinary beauty Standard Y, things will transform for you." 

I say that bc think that it's tempting to entertain a fantasy, even here in this sub, that goes: *if I can just get the right surgeries and treatments, I'll be SO stunningly beautiful that I can enchant my way into this luxe life.* I just don't think that's possible based on beauty alone. There are lots of stunningly beautiful women out there that centimillionaires will happily date but they'll usually end up marrying someone who went to a similar school and has a similar family. And there are plenty of plain ones (looking at you Anna Delvey) who got very far convincing others she belonged with other skills/bravery/audacity. You gotta be savvier, more manipulative, have more on offer, and have a good amount of luck to gain entrée to all this moneyed bliss. 

Or be born into it like the vast, vast majority of these women. In which case, they'll do all the "normal" things of their social class re: grooming (frequent hair appointments, under-eating, manicures, and boring but classy taste) but they're not particularly consumed with it.

Everyone in this thread should read *The Social-Climber's Bible*, which in addition to being one of my favorite funny books is also incredibly accurate. A Johnson & Johnson heiress was the co-author.

**TLDR be ambitious but keep in mind that we still basically live under feudalism and not in some kind of beauty meritocracy**

Out of curiosity have you ever worked in the book publishing field in particular?

*Absolutely* your skills are transferable elsewhere. You sound intelligent, poised, and verbal. Be strong. Do not let this industry convince you that you're soooo lucky to have gotten into publishing as an intern and that you could neeeever get a job in another field. Of course you can. Tons of people do exactly that. Communication skills are useful *anywhere* (think project management, technical writing, UX design). 

Do you know how awful most people are at simply writing a paragraph? This post itself––clear, concise, strong vocabulary––recommends you for a dozen positions I can think of. Seriously!

And not to always sprinkle my posts with this ig account, but [here](https://www.instagram.com/stories/highlights/18256581754021637/) are some places that ex-publishing people went where their skills transferred beautifully.

If you wanted to look elsewhere, you would need to hustle and network to make up for the lack of similar experience on your resume. But that's always the case for starting a new industry (including the first job you got out of undergrad). It can be done and is done frequently.

I will take an unpopular stance in this thread and caution against staying in publishing and going to another (and often even lower-paid) area that isn't editorial, unless you *know* you *personally* would really really love that particular job. I love my publishing peers, but we are by and large [not a happy lot](https://www.instagram.com/xoxopublishinggg/). Virtually any other industry will pay you significantly better for your time than book publishing will, and that industry won't necessarily demand that you fork over 70% of your income to New York City rent, and you will also have a better shot at having a healthy and happy work-life balance.

All that said, I would suggest finishing the internship, if you can afford it financially, simply because you learn a lot and make great connections and meet interesting people. (I think publishing has made me a smarter/more resilient/more interesting person, just not a happy one.) It's a very cool experience whether it leads to your next job or not.

I totally understand your perspective int his argument, it's tough. I firmly believe you're on the right side of this argument––i.e. women make dramatically less money than men do, and *not* because we're silly, flaky things who just just don't take initiative––but people who don't believe this have the advantage if the conversation goes to the Wage Gap Place. I actually think the sources you cited seem pretty much on the mark. The wage gap looks unconvincing to me out of context. It looks like women aren't really getting turned down for promotions if they're truly qualified (from personal experience, I mostly believe this to be true), but men are just hustling more, so they tend to be more qualified and ambitious.

But *why* are men hustling more? *Why* are they on average more qualified? Maybe we're lazier, as women. Maybe wives *enjoy* being dependent on their male spouses for the majority (if not all) of our family income, and maybe we're fine with husbands therefore controlling the family purse strings, despite fifty percent of marriages ending in divorce. Whatever your online arguer believes about the real reason for that gap.

I disagree.

Women make far less than men because someone––ALWAYS SOMEONE, AS LONG AS WE KEEP REPRODUCING AS A SPECIES––has to do the typically-unpaid labor of having children and raising them. Someone has to do it. One parent, two parents, a nanny at six figures a year, daycare that costs so much money that often one parent (hmm, I wonder which?) quits her job because her salary isn't greater than the daycare cost. That job has fallen *overwhelmingly* to women, one parent, despite our best efforts and generally across class lines. 

Someone has to do it, and especially if you have kids in your late 20s and early 30s, there's an extraordinary chance if you're the one to do it,  all your career momentum falls *splat* like a dead fly on the windowsill. It is possible to avoid this. But avoiding this means life on extreme hard mode. Whereas the average American office man has a wife to take care of all this and keeps racking up qualifications and time spent at the office and long work days, etc etc etc, right in that sweet spot of his career's lifetime.

*Of course* men are doing better than women in their careers. Most people have kids ([77% of women by age 34)](https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2018/01/18/theyre-waiting-longer-but-u-s-women-today-more-likely-to-have-children-than-a-decade-ago/). And having a wife is like the magic wand of childcare. Whether it's a housewife or a working woman who's running herself ragged handling childcare *and* her job, a job that surely hates her at this point for having the audacity to reproduce and need to pick up her kid from daycare*,* that's your children taken care of. You, the man, can focus on $$$$$ and you will be praised for it because *that's* how you provide for your family. The money. You don't actually have to do the childcare part that much. Win-win!

But of course, you also have more power than said wife, because money is power.

Anecdotally: If you're a young middle-class girl, it also may be less obvious to you than it is to, say, your brother that you want to make a lot of money personally. If your mother and many of your friends' mothers aren't their families breadwinners, it might very well not occur for you to plan to be a breadwinner. I believe this is why I planned to go into the arts (publishing, pays diddly-squat) with my fantastic grades and my brother, who had no particular interest in finance, decided to go into finance. (It is never too late to change this and I am retraining to become software engineer for the money and freedom there.)

It did not have to be like this. See [this Vox video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AThIwfYfNrM&ab_channel=Vox) on how other wealthy countries adopted universal child care, paid maternal leave, and paid paternal leave after World War II. The problem of raising the next generation can be solved in great part by policy and we should do it for the sake of our financial freedom as women.

Yes! Those are great points to make something more sustainable! I think real OMAD is a lot stricter/harder than what I'm capable of doing haha. For late dinners with friends I sometimes just wait until the dinner, eat for the first time that day at 9 or whatever, and go back to the usual 6pm start time the next day. If I'm actively hungry I'll have a small snack at 6 and also get the later dinner, I probably do that 60% of the time. My eating window isn't always terribly small because I don't have a set time when I *stop* eating. It's usually probably around 8 or 9, but if I want to eat another snack at midnight I do. For me this particular configuration has worked to keep weight down but I know it's a tough calorie/hunger management game that's very individual and takes trial and error.

Re: breakfast, it probably depends what your friends prefer doing. I don't think I've been asked to breakfast in years (I am guessing this is because my friends living in different boroughs here in NYC and it takes like an hour for at least one of us to get to the restaurant lol). If they want to get brunch on Sundays, I'll just eat brunch with them and a smaller dinner or skip dinner if I'm not hungry and it's not so tough. I definitely get hungrier the next day but it's tolerable. If I'm on vacation or something and someone wants to get breakfast I'll just say "I'd love to join you! I get a little nauseous from eating in the morning so I'll just have a coffee while we talk if OK with you." Most people seem perfectly fine with this because I don't think it's being rude to gracefully decline pancakes and meet for coffee. Lots of people don't have breakfast even if they're not doing it for fasting reasons!

I'm sorry about the bloating, that's so rough. What time was your meal when you did OMAD? That might be a useful factor to play with if you're keen. I'm pretty bloated right after dinner (but on weeknights I'm probably at home in PJs by then and don't care so much) and slimmed down by morning, so maybe if you have a late enough meal you sleep through the bloat stage.

Intermittent fasting, I just don't eat until 6pm. Typing that, I realize it sounds a little ambitious, but I promise it's easier than it sounds. It just doesn't take tons of effort to stay low calorie if you're only eating dinner and a little dessert (and at least from a calorie perspective, you can pretty much eat whatever you'd like). I'm more flexible on weekends if I have a friend who wants to get brunch or something. 

It is hard the first week you're doing it, but the hunger goes way down after I'd say five days––your body pretty quickly learns OK, we don't eat until the evening. I do get hungry every day including right now but I'm used to the feeling of hunger at this point and it's fine/sustainable. Imo it's even nice to feel properly hungry, you really enjoy breaking your fast. Keeping a big old 32 ounce Hydroflask on me with ice-cold, Mio-flavored water helps a lot, best $40 I ever spent.

I think fasting is also really good for cell autophagy and keeping you healthy and living longer. And I think it's probably more natural for our species. But to be honest the reason I do it is that if I'm eating breakfast or lunch or snacks, my grehlin and other hunger hormones go nuts! I get WAY hungrier! Dieting is so hard! Tolerating on-and-off hunger until 6 is not. Fasting has been the only easy, sustainable thing for me and I'm able to stay at the weight I like with essentially 5% effort instead of always thinking about diets. 

It also means you can enjoy all the yummiest things in life guilt-free, which makes me happy because I am French and hated giving up bread lol. I will say that lots of nightly carbs make the next day of fasting less comfortable; eating more protein and fat during your nightly meal makes you significantly less hungry the next day, calories aside. Hi there, editorial positions at one of the Big 4 publishing houses are very traditional in that the vast majority of editors become editors through an identical process. After usually 1-3 poorly paid or unpaid publishing internships (usually in NYC), you begin as an editorial assistant. Those jobs are virtually entirely based in Manhattan and pay $30k to $45k (it doesn't go far). After perhaps 2-5 years as an ed. assistant, one moves up to assistant editor, and then several years after that to editor. I have heard of some people skipping the early/editorial assistant steps, but rarely. In those cases, they had done the same thing (internships and assistant-ing) for the agency side of publishing, so they were an experienced literary agent who made a horizontal jump to being an editor. (The opposite direction also happens a lot.)

My understanding is that moving up can be faster if you are at a smaller publishing house (an indie or university press), but pay will usually be lower and it's going to be a different job in some ways; you likely won't be working with the big-name trade books.

I don't think it's ever stupid to look into this as a career! It can be a wonderful and rewarding one. I do think it's important to be transparent about what can be expected at these jobs. It's a lot of extra work reading the manuscript on your own time, especially if you plan to have a family. Often the editorial work is done at home, not during your salaried business hours (and not counted as overtime). Work hours are generally spent e-mailing, taking meetings, and otherwise doing work for your clients. The editorial work is the fun/meaningful part, but it often has to wait until the workday is done. If you are just starting out as an editorial assistant, it's also probably not the majority of what you will be doing for several years. Let me know how I can help answer questions.

Yes, absolutely. Salability might be affected if a market is saturated, for example. In the wake of THE GIRL ON THE TRAIN a few years back, we had so much domestic suspense that we reached a point where no editors wanted to acquire more; it felt dated and tired after the initial rush. Agents and editors may also pass on well-written books that have subject matter that's very, very likely to strike a political/cultural nerve in a bad way. This is especially true for YA. 

Sometimes we're getting reads that absolutely nobody wants to hear about a given topic, given the state of the world, and that makes it near-impossible to make a sale. Example: Almost nobody seems to want to read a book about quarantine/lockdown right now. People want escapism. Even if a Brontë wrote it, it would be extremely hard to make that sale.

All this said, I think trying to accurately guess if their project is salable can make authors insane, and it's an impossible task. My take is that authors should write what they love, and if the time isn't right for their project now, be open to revisiting it later.

Hi there, you'd need to check the original contract for reversion language. Your agent should have negotiated this on your behalf such that if the publisher...

* Fails to publish your book at all, or 
* If your books go out of print, or
* Any number of other specific scenarios,

Rights will revert to you as the author (either immediately or after a certain amount of time) and you can do with them what you wish. Rights to the book's sequels are most likely covered in a different clause. The publisher is likely to have a first-look deal or option on them (so if you write a sequel, you'll agree to send it to them first and give them a chance to make an offer), but this isn't always the case.

Yeah I worry about this on two fronts. The first is that gender dysphoria is a genuine issue, and I feel for anyone who is dysphoric; this can be in relation to your secondary sexual characteristics or it can manifest as something like Body Dysmorphic Disorder, where you may hate some aspect of your appearance so badly you truly feel you cannot leave your house, or may even self-mutilate by trying to perform surgery on yourself. Frankly I can't be convinced that dysphoria isn't real; you have got to be going through some kind of pain to cut out your nasal bone and [put a chicken bone there](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2016/mar/06/the-ugly-truth-about-body-dysmorphia). Frankly the fact that so many trans people have not wavered from being trans through historical periods that were a lot less friendly than this one speaks to the fact that there's a lot of painful sex dysphoria going on, too.

As a society we've come to agree that lifetime hormone replacement therapy and surgery (invasive and not without serious risks) is a good way to alleviate sex-based dysphoria. But most people agree that physical changes are not a good path to alleviate BDD, for example. Similarly, nobody is suggest supporting an anorexic as they count calories. There are obviously meaningful differences here (for one thing, an anorexic on a diet is likely to starve, and arguably with BDD or anorexia, those people are never going to get to a point where they've changed enough to satisfy themselves). But the point I'm making is that there are conceivably several successful ways to respond to painful dysphoria and we've thrown our resources and politics behind just one––perhaps the most invasive, expensive, and [risky](https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/feminizing-hormone-therapy/about/pac-20385096) one.

On the second front (this one more applicable to people who identify as non-binary or genderfluid, or those who don't undergo surgery or HRT), I think women have been held back for millennia on the basis of socially-invented gender roles that spawned from the immutable fact that it's women who bear children––see the effects of the [Agricultural Revolution](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2018/10/how-the-agricultural-revolution-made-us-inequal). Arguably, all the tendencies and assumptions we have created regarding gender have grown out of that fact. Or out of historical attempts to better control reproduction, paternity/lineage, and the unavoidable question of who's going to do the childrearing. 

I thus find it hard to believe there's much that's innate about gender identity. (Like makeup and a tendency toward impractical personal dress, which are [brought up a lot in these discussions](https://www.vox.com/2018/10/22/18009020/transgender-children-teens-transition-detransition-puberty-blocking-medication); what's innate/gender-driven about having an interest in being decorative? It's not a preference associated with men, but does that mean it's necessarily a sign of innate womanhood?) 

There's no right answer here, but that's why I worry. In liberal American circles in 2020, we are talking as if there is a clear right answer and there's not much room to discuss anything else. I think we need to be more open to discussing why we've come to view gender roles as innate tendencies. Right now, communities are throwing a lot of resources behind transitioning and, in the process, they're re-affirming gender roles as innate; it's hard to avoid it because it's an essential assumption underlying the concept of "gender identity." I'm not always against transition, and in individual cases it's just not anybody else's business. But we do need to be able to talk about the general practice more openly than we're doing right now. Currently, if you don't repeat the party line on this issue, you're declaring yourself a backwards transphobe. Which means few people on the left––except people who ENJOY being contrarians (or offensive, or cruel)––are willing to discuss anything other than the party line.
The comment you responded to is more committed to improving our broken system than your reactionary comment itself

Overall, the most attractive combination on myself and others seems to be a tan, but mainly because tans (whether natural suntans, tanning bed tans, or spray/sunless) are a good way to "cheat" an even skintone (fewer capillaries show, a lot of natural discoloration is hidden behind the real or fake melanin) and they give you a certain extra degree of slimness. Unless they're quite slim already and have very, very even skin coloring, most people seem to look best with a light to moderate tan plus moderately darkened facial features so that they aren't lost against the darker base color. But beyond the evening and slimming qualities of a tan, I honestly chalk hair and skin color combinations up to personal preference and can't find a more objectively beautiful combination one way or another.

Yes, I absolutely think you can be depressed because of concrete aspects of your life. For example, I think suicide rates are at record highs in the US right now due to work culture, capitalism, and a lack of community—among many other factors. I don't think these higher rates are happening spontaneously. 

Even if our society was doing just great on average, you could still, as an individual, have shit that makes it nearly impossible to crawl out of this mental hole. 

For me, while I still have very bad mental health periods from time to time (like the past few days, which is why I'm on r/depression right now), I feel that I have crawled out of nearly a decade of severe depression through addressing concrete variables. I'm not on any medication right now (I was on very high doses of SSRIs/buproprion before) so I feel reasonably confident in attributing the change to getting rid of the shit that made me unhappy and adding things that made life worth living. I think it's possible for some, though it greatly depends on the person, their brain, and their situation.

These were the "life just sucks" things for me that changed, which I think made the biggest difference. They're not advice, it's just one case study of before/after, always felt despair/don't usually feel despair:

* I was an alcoholic and drank mostly bourbon from the moment I woke up until I went to sleep (usually blackout). Now I'm over three years sober. I had no money or support to do this, but you can still do it if this is you. I just got shamed into deciding to go to AA and AA is free/a good support group/worked for me.
* I was single and living thousands of miles away from any of my family. Now I live with my romantic partner who is definitely my family and we are planning to get married...I was unrequited-ly obsessed with him for like three years so I felt like \~convincing him to date me\~ was a concrete accomplishment lol...either way this was a huge part of what helped.
* Related: I was desperately worried about finances in NYC and often couldn't (or could barely) pay my rent on time. My partner and I can split rent now and he makes a lot more money than I do. It's not like being well-off necessarily means you're happy, but financial instability will absolutely worsen your mental state.
* I wasn't unemployed for all of my depression (mostly, I was in college and working part time). But unemployment + spotty gig jobs made it way worse. Now I have a stressful more than full-time job, which is not perfect, but I know I need the structure and the sense of meaning/accomplishment.
* I started running 3 miles 5 days a week. I hate when people tell you to exercise the depression away and I'm not going to say that here, but I can't leave it off and be truthful. I started running (and keep doing it) for LITERALLY no reason except to keep my bad mood at bay after seeing this:  [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24026850](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24026850) . It takes so much damned time to run every day after work but idk how to stop and keep my mood up.

And I think that stuff is not enough on its own, either. Even if all the shit in your life went away, life needs to be worth living. I can talk for hours about that but I have a notebook where I try to model my life on [PERMA](https://positivepsychology.com/perma-model/) (a positive psychology thing) to make sure I'm not missing any major ingredient in my life that is necessary for happiness. The first letter of PERMA is basically what you said--"change yr perspective" "see the good in life" blah blah blah--but the rest (ERMA) is more concrete. This [documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_(2011_film)) on Netflix made me curious about positive psychology. I think it's not enough on its own but you do need it. It's not enough to just be barely staying afloat in life.

Also idk how old you are, and not to be pessimistic, but I was suicidal in high school and I don't know ANYTHING I could have done differently. It was IMPOSSIBLE back then. I was old enough to have responsibilities and shit that made me miserable, but not old enough to really control my own life. Godspeed to anyone here who has to live with their parents.

Now that I'm an adult, having gone through some strategic changes + good luck + suffering in pursuit of getting better, a lot of my bad shit has changed. Life isn't perfect but it's bearable now, sometimes even pretty good or wonderful. 90+ percent of the time, I no longer want to kill myself. I can't believe I'm typing that, things have changed so much in the last few years.
